title: Claim: linked-list-no-random-access
body: A linked list requires O(n) steps to reach a position, so binary search is impossible without modifying the structure.

title: Claim: linked-list-insert-delete-constant
body: Insertion and deletion at a known node (with a pointer to it) cost O(1), because no shifting is required.

title: Claim: reversal-redirects-pointers-inplace
body: Reversing a linked list in-place by redirecting pointers uses O(1) extra space and O(n) time.

title: Claim: cycle-detection-two-pointers
body: A cycle in a linked list can be detected by advancing two pointers at different speeds; if they meet, a cycle exists.

title: Claim: dummy-node-simplifies-head-cases
body: A dummy node pointing to the head eliminates special cases when modifying the head node.

title: Q1: Why is reversal a natural fit for linked lists?
body:
A. Linked lists are smaller than arrays
B. Pointers can be redirected in-place without allocating new nodes, using O(1) extra space
C. Reversing arrays requires copying the entire array
D. Linked lists are always bidirectional

**B.** Reversing a linked list changes the direction of pointers, not the nodes themselves. This in-place redirection uses constant extra space.

title: Q2: How does the two-pointer cycle detection algorithm work?
body:
A. Mark visited nodes with a flag
B. Use a set to track seen nodes
C. Advance two pointers at different speeds; they meet if a cycle exists
D. Count nodes and check if the count exceeds the list length

**C.** A fast pointer (2 steps per iteration) and a slow pointer (1 step) eventually meet if a cycle exists. If the fast pointer reaches null, there is no cycle.

title: Q3: Why is a dummy node useful when merging linked lists?
body:
A. It makes the list shorter
B. It holds the smaller of the two heads
C. It eliminates special cases at the head by providing a node to attach to initially
D. It is required by the algorithm

**C.** A dummy node lets the merge code treat the head uniformly. Instead of checking 'is this the first node?', the code always attaches to the previous node.

title: Q4: In the 'Merge K Sorted Lists' problem, why is a heap faster
body:
A. Heaps use less memory
B. Heaps sort the lists automatically
C. Finding the next smallest among k lists is O(log k) with a heap instead of O(k) with linear search
D. Heaps eliminate the need for pointers

**C.** A heap tracks the smallest head across k lists. Inserting and extracting takes O(log k) per step, making the total time O(n log k) instead of O(n * k).

title: Q5: What is the time complexity of traversing a linked list to f
body:
A. O(1)
B. O(log n)
C. O(n)
D. O(n log n)

**C.** A linked list has no random access. Reaching a node requires following pointers from the head, which takes O(n) in the worst case.
